title: US one-off transfers produced a delayed, hump-shaped consumption response
source_unit: US veterans, postwar transfer payments, household consumption, transfer timing, cumulative transfer multiplier, and expectations
geography: United States; post-World War II veteran payment natural experiment

observations.period: Working paper issued September 2026; postwar US veterans’ payments

denominator.unit: US veterans and households receiving plausibly exogenous postwar payments; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

consumption_path.unit: one-off transfers produce a temporary transfer increase followed by a persistent, hump-shaped increase in consumption

multiplier_six_months.unit: cumulative consumption response per dollar of transfer after six months

multiplier_one_year.unit: cumulative consumption response per dollar of transfer after one year

transfer_design.unit: one-off, deficit-financed lump-sum payments to households

expectations.unit: households underreact on impact but overreact at longer horizons in the model matching the consumption estimates

observations.method: A natural experiment uses plausibly exogenous payments to US veterans after World War II, estimating the dynamic consumption response and comparing it with heterogeneous-agent macroeconomic models.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose sample counts, confidence intervals, exact payment size, consumption measures, or all identification assumptions. Historical veteran payments may not generalize to current households, and a consumption multiplier is not the same as food security, debt reduction, health, durable security, or equal welfare.
observations.subgroup: US veterans and households receiving postwar payments, with dynamic responses measured over six months and one year.
observations.counterinterpretation: Payments, wartime institutions, household balance sheets, expectations, prices, supply constraints, and veteran eligibility may differ from modern stimulus programs; aggregate consumption can rise while some households remain constrained or face later repayment and fiscal effects.

related_sources.claim: P-EBT disbursements increased sugary-item spending among eligible households with school-aged children.
SNAP restrictions reduced restricted spending, calories, and sugar while creating substitution and channel effects.
Low-income and low-skill workers show persistent labor-force exit and limited replacement of lost W-2 income.

boundary: This record adds a dynamic transfer-to-consumption layer to the US consumer program. It does not establish modern stimulus effects, household security, nutrition, debt, health, political trust, or equal welfare, and the one-year multiplier is not a direct measure of durable benefit.
